This breaks the intuition that an insolvent institution must fail. A normal company that owes more than it owns is bankrupt. A central bank's liabilities are its own banknotes and reserves, which it issues, so it cannot be forced into default in its own currency the way a household or firm can.

The real constraint isn't solvency but inflation and credibility. If a central bank prints to cover its losses recklessly, it can debase the currency and lose public trust, which is the thing that actually matters. So the limit is political and economic, not accounting. It's a useful reminder that 'running out of money' means something completely different for the issuer of money than for the rest of us.

headline: Giffen goods: when a price rise makes you buy more
body: Economics says demand falls as price rises, but a rare exception exists. For a Giffen good, a staple so dominant in a poor household's budget that a price rise makes them too poor to afford anything else, demand can actually increase.
more:
Imagine a family that survives mostly on rice plus the occasional bit of meat. If rice gets more expensive, the family becomes poorer overall, can no longer afford the meat, and must fill the calorie gap with even more cheap rice. The price went up and they bought more of it.

For over a century these were textbook curiosities with no solid real-world proof. Then in the 2000s, economists Robert Jensen and Nolan Miller ran field experiments in poor regions of China and found genuine Giffen behaviour for rice and wheat among the very poor. It's a striking demonstration that the most basic 'law' of demand has an edge case, hiding precisely where people are too poor to have alternatives.

headline: Hyperinflation can make burning cash cheaper than firewood
body: In Germany's 1923 hyperinflation, prices doubled every few days. People famously found it cheaper to burn banknotes for warmth than to buy firewood, and wallpapered rooms with worthless marks.
more:
Workers were paid twice a day and rushed to spend the money before lunchtime, because by evening it bought half as much. Restaurants stopped printing prices on menus; the figure changed during the meal. A wheelbarrow of cash could be stolen by tipping out the money and taking the barrow.

The deeper mechanism is a vicious feedback loop: once people expect money to lose value, they spend it instantly, which speeds up its circulation and drives prices up further, fuelling the very expectation. This is why central bankers treat inflation expectations as something to defend almost above all else. The currency stabilised only when a new mark was introduced, credibly backed and limited in supply, restoring the one thing money truly runs on, which is belief.

headline: The man who tried to corner the silver market
body: In 1979-80 the Hunt brothers, Texas oil heirs, quietly bought up so much silver that they controlled a large share of the world's supply, driving the price from about 6 dollars to nearly 50 an ounce.
more:
Cornering a market means owning enough of a commodity that you can dictate its price, forcing anyone who needs it to buy from you. The Hunts borrowed heavily to keep buying, and as silver soared, ordinary people melted down family heirlooms to sell.

The scheme unravelled when exchanges changed the rules, restricting how much silver could be bought on borrowed money. The price collapsed in a single day later called Silver Thursday, the Hunts faced enormous margin calls they couldn't meet, and one of America's richest families was driven toward bankruptcy. The episode shows both the temptation and the fatal flaw of cornering: you need ever more borrowed money to hold the corner, and the moment the rules or sentiment shift, leverage that built the position destroys it.

headline: Vending machines invented one of the first anti-fraud sensors
body: Coin-operated machines had to solve a hard problem early: telling a real coin from a slug. The mechanisms inside became surprisingly sophisticated, checking a coin's size, weight, and even its magnetic and electrical properties.
more:
A modern coin acceptor rolls the coin past sensors that measure its diameter and run it through a magnetic field; the way a genuine coin's alloy interacts with that field produces a signature that's hard to fake with a washer or a foreign coin of the same size. Reject the coin and it drops into the return cup.

This is a tiny, everyday example of the same arms race that runs through all of commerce: every payment system, from coins to credit cards to crypto, is a contest between people trying to authenticate value cheaply and people trying to counterfeit it. The vending machine just had to win that contest with no human in the loop, decades before 'fraud detection' became a software industry.

headline: Ketchup, mustard and the razor-and-blades trap
body: Selling the razor cheap and the blades dear is a classic business model: lock customers into a cheap base product, then profit from the expensive consumables they're forced to keep buying. Printers and ink are the modern poster child.
more:
The trick only works if you can stop customers buying cheaper third-party refills, which is why companies fight hard with chips, patents and warranties to keep rivals out of the 'blades' market. When that lock-in fails, the whole model collapses, because you sold the base product at a loss expecting to recoup it later.

There's a twist worth knowing: Gillette, the company the strategy is named after, may not actually have priced its early razors cheaply at all. The neat origin story is partly retrofitted. But the underlying logic is sound and everywhere, from coffee pods to game consoles sold below cost to make money on the games. Whenever a base product seems suspiciously cheap, ask where the recurring revenue is hiding.

headline: The bank that failed because of a rogue spreadsheet... and worse
body: Barings, a 230-year-old British bank that had financed the Napoleonic Wars and the Louisiana Purchase, was destroyed in 1995 by the unsupervised trades of a single 28-year-old, who hid his losses in an account numbered 88888.
more: The story is a full thread on its own; the short version is that one man controlled both the trading and the settlement of his own deals, the textbook recipe for disaster. With no one checking his work, small losses could be buried and then doubled down on in a desperate attempt to win them back, until the hole swallowed the entire bank.

headline: How a single trader broke a 230-year-old bank →
body: Nick Leeson was Barings' star trader in Singapore, seemingly generating huge profits. He was also, quietly, the man who checked his own trades. That combination is how one person erased a bank older than most countries' constitutions.

headline: The account numbered 88888
body: Leeson opened a secret 'error account' numbered 88888 and used it to hide trading losses from London. Eight is a lucky number in Chinese culture; the account became the opposite, a black hole that grew as he bet bigger to recover.

headline: Both the trader and the referee
body: The fatal flaw was structural. Leeson ran the trading desk and the back office that settled and verified those trades. With no separation of duties, he could fake the paperwork that should have caught him, the single control that might have saved the bank.
more: This is why every serious financial institution now enforces 'segregation of duties': the person who makes a deal must never be the person who confirms and records it. The principle long predates Barings, but Barings is why it's drilled into every compliance course. One person wearing both hats can hide almost anything, for a while.

headline: An earthquake finished it
body: Leeson had made an enormous bet that Japan's stock market would stay calm. On 17 January 1995 the Kobe earthquake struck, markets lurched, and his hidden position spiralled. By late February the losses topped 800 million pounds, more than the bank's entire capital.
more:
Barings was sold to the Dutch bank ING for the symbolic sum of one pound, its 233-year history ended. Leeson fled, was arrested, and served years in a Singapore prison. He later wrote a memoir and, in a final irony of the lecture circuit, now gives talks on risk management.

The lasting lesson isn't about one greedy man; it's about systems. The losses didn't come from a brilliant fraud but from ordinary controls that simply weren't there. A junior employee with no oversight, doubling down to escape losses, is a pattern that has recurred at far bigger banks since. The names change; the missing referee does not.

headline: The strangest corporate collapse: a company worth more empty →
body: Some companies have been worth more dead than alive, their breakup value exceeding their stock price. But stranger still are firms that collapsed not from losses but from accounting fictions, where the profits themselves were never real.

headline: Booking tomorrow's profit today
body: Enron pioneered 'mark-to-market' accounting for long-term energy deals: the moment it signed a 20-year contract, it booked the entire projected profit immediately, based on its own forecasts. If reality fell short, the gap had to be hidden somewhere.
more: Once you can record profit you merely predict, every incentive bends toward optimistic forecasts. Sign a bigger, longer deal, claim a bigger profit now, hit your targets, collect your bonus. The trouble is that the cash hasn't arrived and may never. The reported earnings become a story about the future dressed as a fact about the present.

headline: Hiding the debt in companies that didn't quite exist
body: To bury the resulting losses and debts, Enron shuffled them into hundreds of 'special purpose entities', shell companies that were technically separate but secretly backed by Enron's own stock. The debt vanished from the books while remaining very much real.
more: The scheme worked only as long as Enron's share price stayed high, because the shells were propped up by that stock. It was a financial perpetual-motion machine that depended on never stopping. When the share price began to fall, the hidden structures unravelled all at once, and the losses they concealed came flooding back onto the balance sheet they were designed to protect.

headline: The fall took the auditor down too
body: Enron collapsed into bankruptcy in 2001, wiping out thousands of employees' pensions, which had been heavily invested in its own stock. The scandal also destroyed Arthur Andersen, one of the world's five largest accounting firms, which had signed off on the books.
more:
Andersen was convicted (later overturned on a technicality, but too late) of obstructing justice for shredding Enron documents, and effectively ceased to exist, taking tens of thousands of innocent jobs with it. The episode directly produced the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which forced executives to personally certify their financial statements.

The enduring lesson is about the chain of trust. Investors trusted the auditor; the auditor was paid by the company it audited, a principal-agent conflict baked into the system. When the watchdog depends on the goodwill of the thing it watches, the watching gets soft. Enron didn't just expose one rotten company; it exposed how many guardrails quietly depend on everyone choosing not to look too hard.

headline: Inflation can be good for some borrowers
body: Unexpected inflation quietly transfers wealth from lenders to borrowers. If you owe a fixed-rate sum and money loses value, you repay your debt in cheaper future dollars, while your lender gets back less than they thought they lent.
more:
This is why a homeowner with a fixed-rate mortgage can secretly benefit from a burst of inflation: their wages and home price tend to rise with the price level, but their monthly payment stays frozen in old money. Savers holding cash and bonds, by contrast, lose.

Governments are among the biggest fixed-rate borrowers, which is one reason economists watch carefully for the temptation to 'inflate away' national debt. The flip side is that lenders aren't naive: once they expect inflation, they demand higher interest rates to compensate, so only the surprise portion of inflation actually does the wealth-transfer. Anticipated inflation just gets priced in.

headline: Why airlines overbook on purpose
body: Airlines routinely sell more seats than the plane has. It looks reckless, but it's a calculated bet: a predictable fraction of passengers never show up, so selling those empty seats twice fills planes that would otherwise fly with costly gaps.
more:
The math is a straightforward expected-value calculation. The airline knows roughly what percentage of a given route's passengers no-show, and overbooks by close to that amount. On the rare flight where everyone turns up, it pays volunteers to take a later flight, a cost it has already budgeted for and which is usually far smaller than the revenue gained across thousands of flights.

The practice became infamous when overbooking met poor execution and passengers were forcibly removed, but the underlying logic is sound risk pooling. It's the same statistical reasoning a casino or insurer uses: you can't predict any single person's behaviour, but across enough people the aggregate is remarkably stable and therefore profitable to bet on.

headline: The Cobra Effect: a bounty that bred more cobras
body: Under British rule in Delhi, officials worried about cobras offered a bounty for dead snakes. Enterprising locals responded rationally, by breeding cobras to kill for the reward. When the scheme was scrapped, the now-worthless snakes were released, leaving more cobras than before.
more:
Whether every detail is documented or partly legend, the pattern is real and well-attested elsewhere: a French bounty on rat tails in colonial Hanoi led people to farm rats, and to cut tails off live rats so they could keep breeding.

The Cobra Effect is the vivid cousin of Goodhart's Law: reward a proxy ('dead cobras') instead of the goal ('fewer cobras'), and people will manufacture the proxy. The deeper design lesson is to anticipate the supply response. Any incentive doesn't just change how people behave with the existing world; it changes what world they choose to create. Pay for a thing and you'll get more of that thing, including in ways you never intended.

headline: Most day traders lose money, consistently
body: Study after study finds that the large majority of active individual day traders lose money over time, and only a tiny fraction beat a simple index fund after costs. The losers don't vanish quietly; new ones keep arriving, sure they'll be the exception.
more:
A landmark study of the entire Taiwanese market over several years found that fewer than 1 percent of day traders were reliably profitable after fees, and the typical trader lost money. Frequent trading is a near-perfect machine for converting your capital into brokerage and spread costs.

Why does the belief persist? Survivorship bias and selective memory. The handful who win post their gains loudly; the many who lose go quiet and quit. Trading platforms and finance media amplify the winners because excitement drives engagement. The boring truth, that most people are best served by cheap diversified funds they rarely touch, makes for terrible content and excellent results.

headline: The 'Big Mac Index' was a joke that became a real tool
body: The Economist invented the Big Mac Index in 1986 as a lighthearted way to gauge whether currencies were over- or undervalued, by comparing the local price of a Big Mac around the world. The joke proved useful enough that economists now cite it seriously.
more:
The idea rests on 'purchasing power parity': the same basket of goods should, in theory, cost the same everywhere once you convert currencies. A Big Mac is a clever stand-in basket because it's nearly identical worldwide and bundles local labour, rent, meat, and bread into one price. If a burger is far cheaper in one country, its currency may be undervalued against the dollar.

It's imperfect (local wages, taxes and beef prices all distort it), but it captures a real principle in a way anyone can grasp. The lasting point is methodological: a transparent, dead-simple proxy that everyone understands can sometimes beat a sophisticated model that few can check. Burgernomics earned its place by being honest about its own crudeness.

headline: Prediction markets often beat the experts
body: When you let people bet real money on uncertain outcomes, the resulting market prices frequently forecast events, elections, product launches, project deadlines, more accurately than panels of experts or internal forecasts.
more:
The mechanism is that betting forces honesty. In a meeting, people hedge, defer to the boss, or echo the room. In a market, a confident wrong opinion costs you money, so participants weigh their true beliefs and stake accordingly. The price aggregates thousands of these incentivised guesses into a single number.

Companies like Google and HP ran internal prediction markets where employees anonymously bet on whether projects would ship on time, and found them sharper than official timelines, partly because they surfaced the quiet pessimism managers don't like to hear. The limits are real (thin markets, manipulation, taboo questions), but the core insight is powerful: skin in the game is a remarkably effective truth serum.

headline: Why your loyalty card is worth more than the discount it gives
body: Supermarket loyalty cards hand you small discounts, but the real prize flows the other way: detailed data on exactly what you buy, when, and how price changes shift your behaviour. The discount is the price the store pays for that information.
more:
With your purchase history, retailers can predict life events, a shift in buying suggests a new baby or a move, and target offers accordingly. One famous case had a retailer's models inferring a teenager's pregnancy from her shopping before her family knew. Aggregated across millions of shoppers, this data lets stores fine-tune prices, placement and promotions with surgical precision.

The deeper point is a recurring one in the modern economy: when a service is cheap or free, you are often paying with data rather than money, and data, unlike cash, can be copied, combined and sold endlessly. The 'discount' is real, but it's the bait in a transaction where the more valuable asset is you.

headline: Veblen goods: raise the price and sell more
body: For most things, a higher price means fewer buyers. But some luxury goods are Veblen goods, where a high price is the point. Make the watch or handbag more expensive and demand can rise, because the cost is what signals status.
more:
Named after economist Thorstein Veblen, who coined 'conspicuous consumption', these goods work as signals precisely because they're expensive. A handbag that anyone could afford couldn't communicate wealth, so cutting the price would destroy the very thing customers are buying. This is why luxury brands guard against discounting and sometimes destroy unsold stock rather than mark it down.

It overturns the basic demand curve in a specific, social way: the buyer's true product isn't the leather or the mechanism, it's the visible signal of being able to waste money. That makes such markets strange. A rival can't compete by being cheaper; cheaper is worse. The only way to win is to be even more exclusive, which is a very different game from ordinary commerce.

headline: The tragedy of the commons isn't inevitable
body: When many people share a resource no one owns, a pasture, a fishery, the atmosphere, each is tempted to take a bit more, and collectively they ruin it. But the famous conclusion that this is unavoidable without top-down control turned out to be too pessimistic.
more:
Elinor Ostrom won the 2009 Nobel in economics for documenting hundreds of real communities, Swiss alpine herders, Japanese forest villagers, Spanish irrigation networks, that managed shared resources sustainably for centuries without privatising them or being ruled by a distant authority. They did it with their own homegrown rules, monitoring, and graduated penalties for cheats.

The lesson rewrites a famous bit of conventional wisdom. The 'tragedy' is a risk, not a law of nature. What prevents it is neither pure markets nor pure government but a third thing: trusted local institutions where the people who use a resource also make and enforce the rules for it. It's a hopeful and underappreciated finding about how humans actually cooperate.

headline: The Soviet nail factory paradox
body: A factory is told to maximise the number of nails it produces. What does it most likely make?
options: A balanced mix of useful nail sizes
A vast number of tiny, useless nails
A few enormous, useless nails
Exactly the nails customers need
explanation: Judged on count, the factory makes millions of tiny nails nobody can use. (Judged on weight, it makes a few giant ones.) Either way the metric is hit and the goal is missed, a perfect illustration of Goodhart's Law: once a measure becomes a target, people optimise the measure, not the goal.

headline: Which planes should you armour?
body: Returning WWII bombers show bullet holes mostly on the wings and tail, rarely on the engines. To improve survival, where should you add armour?
options: The wings and tail, where the holes are
The engines, where the holes aren't
Spread armour evenly everywhere
Add no armour; it adds weight
explanation: Armour the engines. You only see planes that came back; ones hit in the engines didn't return to be studied. The unscarred areas mark the fatal hits. This is survivorship bias, and Abraham Wald's reasoning saved many aircrew.

headline: The lawyer and the typist
body: A lawyer can type faster than any assistant she could hire, and her legal work is far more valuable than typing. Should she do her own typing?
options: Yes, since she's faster, she's the best person for it
No, her time is better spent on legal work
Yes, to save money on an assistant
It makes no economic difference either way
explanation: She should hire the slower typist. Every hour she types costs her an hour of much more valuable legal work. The assistant has the comparative advantage in typing, despite the lawyer's absolute advantage, because the assistant gives up far less to do it. Relative opportunity cost, not raw skill, decides who should do what.

headline: You win the oil-lease auction. Now worry.
body: Several firms bid for drilling rights of unknown value, each using its own estimate. You win. What's the most rational immediate concern?
options: That you bid too little and barely won
That you probably overestimated the value and overpaid
That the other firms colluded against you
Nothing; winning means you valued it correctly
explanation: This is the winner's curse. In a common-value auction, the winner is usually the bidder who most overestimated the prize, so winning is itself a signal you overpaid. The rational defence is to shade your bid below your own estimate, conditioning on the bad news that winning implies.

headline: The non-refundable concert ticket
body: You paid 40 dollars for a concert tonight. Now you feel unwell and would honestly rather stay home. The money is non-refundable. What should you do?
options: Go, so the 40 dollars isn't wasted
Stay home, since the 40 dollars is gone either way
Go, because you already committed
It depends on whether the ticket could be resold tonight
explanation: Stay home if that's what you'd genuinely prefer. The 40 dollars is a sunk cost: unrecoverable, and identical whether you go or not. Only the forward-looking choice matters. Going purely to 'not waste' money already spent is the sunk-cost fallacy. (If the ticket were resellable, that changes the math, but the original payment still shouldn't.)

headline: Where does most money come from?
body: In a modern economy, who creates the bulk of the money in circulation?
options: The central bank, by printing physical cash
The government, through taxation
Commercial banks, by making loans
Mints, by producing coins and notes
explanation: Most money is created by ordinary commercial banks when they make loans, typing new deposits into existence rather than relending savers' cash. The Bank of England said so plainly in 2014. Physical notes and coins are a small fraction of the money supply.

headline: The used car you can't inspect
body: Buyers can't tell good used cars from hidden lemons, so they offer only an average price. Over time, what happens to the cars on the market?
options: Quality rises as sellers compete
Good cars leave and quality falls toward lemons
Prices and quality both climb
Nothing changes; the market stays balanced
explanation: Owners of good cars refuse the mediocre average price and exit, while owners of lemons happily sell. The average quality drops, the price drops further, and the market can unravel. This is Akerlof's lemons problem, caused by asymmetric information. Warranties, certifications and reputations exist to close that information gap.

headline: Why does a haircut keep getting more expensive?
body: Over decades, services like haircuts, live music and teaching rise in price faster than manufactured goods like TVs. What best explains it?
options: Service workers are simply greedier over time
These jobs can't easily get more productive, yet must match economy-wide wage growth
Demand for services keeps falling
Governments tax services more heavily
explanation: This is Baumol's cost disease. A barber or string quartet can't produce much more per hour than decades ago, but to keep workers from leaving for sectors where productivity (and pay) is soaring, their wages must rise too. So labour-intensive services get relatively more expensive, a side effect of overall economic progress.

headline: The bounty that backfired
body: Colonial officials offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra to reduce the snake population. What was the likely result?
options: The cobra population fell sharply as planned
People bred cobras to claim bounties, worsening the problem
The bounty was too small to change anything
Cobras migrated away from the city
explanation: People began breeding cobras to kill for the reward. When the scheme ended, the now-worthless snakes were released, leaving more cobras than before, the Cobra Effect. Rewarding a proxy (dead cobras) instead of the real goal (fewer cobras) invites people to manufacture the proxy. Always anticipate the supply response to an incentive.

headline: Whose house sits on the market longer?
body: Research compared homes that real-estate agents sold for clients versus homes the agents owned themselves. What did it find?
options: Agents sold their own homes faster and for less
Agents kept their own homes on the market longer and sold them for more
No measurable difference between the two
Agents sold client homes for higher prices
explanation: Agents left their own homes on the market longer and got higher prices, exactly what the principal-agent problem predicts. On a client's sale, the agent does most of the extra work to chase a higher price but pockets only a sliver of the gain via commission, so they're biased toward a fast, easy sale instead.

headline: Why can an index fund beat the stock-pickers?
body: An index fund analyses no companies at all, yet outperforms most active managers over time. Why does this work?
options: It secretly times the market better
It free-rides on prices set by active traders while keeping fees tiny
Companies in indexes are chosen for quality
Index funds take on far more risk for higher returns
explanation: Active investors do the costly work of researching companies and setting roughly fair prices. The index fund accepts those prices, owns the whole market cheaply, and avoids the fees and trading costs that drag down active funds. It free-rides on others' price discovery, a strategy that only works because enough active traders still bother to do that work.

headline: Your body is a Ship of Theseus that finishes refitting every few years
body: The ancient puzzle asks: if you replace every plank of a ship one by one, is it still the same ship? Your body runs this experiment for real. Most of your cells and nearly all the atoms in them are swapped out over a span of years. The 'you' reading this shares almost no physical material with the 'you' of a decade ago.
more:
The point isn't a trivia fact about cells. It's that personal identity can't be the matter you're made of, because the matter keeps changing while 'you' persist. So what does the continuity consist of? Candidates include the pattern (the arrangement, not the stuff), psychological continuity (overlapping chains of memory and intention), and bodily continuity (the same gradually-changing organism).

This matters in practice. It's why we hold people responsible for promises made years ago, why a teleporter that destroyed and rebuilt you would feel terrifying even if the copy were perfect, and why brain-continuity matters to us more than, say, kidney-continuity. The Ship of Theseus isn't solved by picking the 'right' answer; it's solved by noticing that 'same' is a word we apply for different purposes, and the purpose decides the answer.

headline: Chesterton's Fence: don't remove what you don't understand
body: G.K. Chesterton imagined a fence across a road with no obvious purpose. The reformer says 'I see no use for this; let's clear it away.' The wiser reply: 'If you don't see its use, I won't let you remove it. Go away and think. Then when you can tell me you DO see its use, I may let you destroy it.'
more:
The rule isn't 'never change anything.' It's a sequencing rule: understand why a thing exists before you tear it out. Many rules, processes, and odd workarounds are scar tissue from a real problem someone already solved. Remove the fence and the bull comes back.

In engineering this is the legacy code you're tempted to delete because it 'looks pointless.' In organizations it's the approval step that seems like bureaucracy until you learn which disaster it was created to prevent. The practical move: when something seems dumb, treat that feeling as a flag that you're missing context, not as proof you're smarter. Find the original reason first. Sometimes the reason is genuinely obsolete and you remove the fence with confidence. Sometimes you discover the bull.

headline: The Experience Machine: would you plug in?
body: Robert Nozick asked: imagine a machine that could give you any experience you desired, perfectly real from the inside, for the rest of your life. You'd never know you were plugged in. Pure bliss on tap. Would you do it? Most people recoil and say no.
more:
That refusal is the philosophical payload. If pleasure were the only thing we valued, plugging in would be a no-brainer. The fact that most people won't suggests we want more than the feeling of doing things; we want to actually do them, to actually connect with real people, to actually be a certain kind of person rather than just float in a tank believing we are.

Nozick used it as an argument against hedonism, the view that pleasure is the only good. The thought experiment is sharper today: streaming, games, and engineered feeds are partial experience machines. Noticing that you wouldn't plug in fully is a useful test for how much of your real life you're already trading for the feeling of a life.

headline: Mary's Room: knowing every fact about red, but never seeing it
body: Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who knows every physical fact about color vision, all the wavelengths and neuroscience, but has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. One day she walks outside and sees a red rose. Does she learn something new?
more:
Intuitively, yes: she learns what red looks like. But if she already knew every physical fact and still learned something, then there's a fact about experience that isn't captured by physics. This is the 'knowledge argument' against physicalism, the claim that everything is physical.

The debate is unresolved and contested. Some say Mary gains a new ability (to recognize, imagine, remember red) rather than a new fact. Some say she knew the fact in one form and now knows it 'from the inside.' Jackson himself later changed his mind and rejected his own argument. The lasting value is the wedge it drives into the 'consciousness is just information processing' story: knowing the full description of an experience seems different from having it, and nobody has cleanly explained why.

headline: Newcomb's Problem: a paradox that splits rational people in two
body: Two boxes. Box A holds $1,000, visible. Box B holds either $1,000,000 or nothing. You may take both boxes, or just Box B. The catch: a near-perfect predictor already filled Box B with the million ONLY if it predicted you'd take B alone. It has already decided and left. What do you take?
more:
'Two-boxers' reason: the predictor is gone, the money is already in or out, so taking both strictly dominates. You get whatever's in B plus a guaranteed extra $1,000. This is the logic of causal decision theory: your choice now can't reach back and change a sealed box.

'One-boxers' note that everyone who took both boxes walked away with $1,000, and everyone who took one walked away with $1,000,000. If you're the kind of agent who two-boxes, the predictor knew that and left B empty. The disagreement is genuine and deep; it's about whether rationality should track causation or correlation with your own decision-making. It surfaces in real life as 'voting feels pointless because one vote can't change the outcome' versus 'people like me deciding it's pointless is exactly how elections are lost.'

headline: The Veil of Ignorance: design the world before you know who you'll be
body: John Rawls asked: what rules for society would you choose if you didn't know who you'd be in it, your class, race, talents, health, or religion? Behind this 'veil of ignorance,' self-interest and fairness collapse into the same thing, because any group you disadvantage might turn out to be you.
more:
Rawls argued that rational people behind the veil would protect the worst-off positions, because they couldn't risk being stuck there. He called this the 'difference principle': inequalities are only justified if they improve the situation of the least advantaged. You'd accept doctors earning more if that incentive produces better healthcare for everyone, but not inequality that just entrenches privilege.

As a practical tool it's portable beyond grand politics. Designing a refund policy, a layoff process, a group's chore split? Ask what you'd choose if you didn't know which role you'd land in. It strips out the self-serving thumb on the scale. Critics note it may push people to be more risk-averse than real humans are, and that 'rational choice behind the veil' smuggles in assumptions. But as a debiasing move, it's one of the most useful inventions in modern ethics.

headline: The Trolley Problem isn't about trolleys
body: A runaway trolley will kill five people. You can pull a lever to divert it to a track where it kills one. Most say pull. Now: the only way to stop it is to push a large stranger off a bridge into its path, killing him to save five. Same math, but most people refuse. Why?
more:
The numbers are identical; the intuition flips. Philippa Foot and Judith Jarvis Thomson used the contrast to expose that we don't reason about ethics by arithmetic alone. Something about using a person as a physical means to an end, touching them, treating them as a tool, feels categorically different from redirecting a harm that's already in motion.

This maps onto a real fault line: consequentialism (judge by outcomes) versus deontology (some acts are wrong regardless of outcome). The practical payoff isn't picking a side; it's recognizing that policy debates often hide a trolley problem. 'We could save more lives by reallocating this budget' is a lever-pull argument. 'But that means actively sacrificing those specific identifiable people' is the bridge. Knowing which one you're being asked to do clarifies a lot of arguments that otherwise feel like people talking past each other.

headline: Hume's guillotine: you can't derive an 'ought' from an 'is'
body: David Hume noticed that arguments often slide from statements of fact ('this is how things are') to statements of value ('this is how things ought to be') without ever justifying the jump. No pile of facts, by itself, logically forces a conclusion about what you should do.
more:
This is why a debate about, say, immigration or diet never gets settled by data alone. The facts constrain the options, but they don't tell you which goal to weight. 'Natural' doesn't mean 'good.' 'It's efficient' doesn't mean 'do it' unless you've already valued efficiency. There's always a hidden value premise carrying the weight.

The practical skill is spotting the smuggled 'ought.' When someone says 'studies show X, therefore we must do Y,' find the missing premise: 'and we value Z.' Usually the real disagreement lives there, in the values, not the studies, which is why throwing more data at a values fight rarely works. It also inoculates you against the appeal-to-nature and appeal-to-science moves that dress a preference up as a fact.

headline: Pascal's Mugging: when tiny probabilities times huge payoffs break your math
body: Pascal argued you should believe in God because even a small chance of infinite reward outweighs any finite cost. The 'mugging' version turns this against itself: a stranger says 'give me $5 or I'll use magic powers to cause unimaginable suffering to trillions.' The threat is absurd, but the stakes are so vast that any nonzero probability seems to demand you pay.
more:
It exposes a real bug in naive expected-value reasoning. If you multiply a tiny probability by a large enough payoff, the product can swamp everything, so a sufficiently grandiose claim can hijack your decisions. Con artists, fearmongers, and some apocalyptic arguments exploit exactly this shape.

The practical defense: be suspicious when someone scales the payoff toward infinity to make the probability irrelevant. Real reasoning needs a way to discount claims whose probability is itself only supported by the size of the prize. It also clarifies Pascal's original wager: the flaw isn't the logic of the bet but that you can construct infinitely many mutually exclusive infinite-payoff gods, and the argument gives you no way to choose between them.

headline: The Stoic dichotomy of control is a productivity tool in disguise
body: Epictetus, who was born enslaved, taught that some things are 'up to us' (our judgments, choices, effort) and some are not (the weather, other people's opinions, outcomes). Nearly all suffering, he argued, comes from trying to control the second category and neglecting the first.
more:
This is not passive resignation. It's a sorting algorithm for attention. Spend your energy entirely on the move, not the result; on your preparation, not the verdict; on how you respond, not what happened. The outcome is the universe's business once you've done your part.

Modern cognitive behavioral therapy descends directly from this. The practical version for work: separate 'did I do good work and act with integrity' (yours) from 'did it get approved, did it go viral, did they like me' (not yours). Caring about results is fine; staking your peace on results you don't control is the trap. The Stoics didn't stop wanting things; they stopped letting the wanting hold their inner state hostage.

headline: The Halo Effect explains why we trust attractive liars
body: One good trait bleeds into our judgment of unrelated traits. We rate good-looking people as more honest, competent, and kind, with no evidence for any of it. The effect was first documented in army officers rating soldiers: officers who were rated good at one thing got rated good at everything, in lockstep.
more:
It's a perception bug, not a moral failing, and it runs in reverse too (the 'horn effect'): one flaw taints everything. This is why confident, articulate people get away with weak arguments, why a polished slide deck makes a bad plan feel solid, and why a single typo can sink an otherwise excellent application.

The defense is to evaluate traits separately and deliberately. When hiring, score each competency on its own before forming an overall impression. When persuaded by someone, ask whether you're convinced by the argument or by the person's poise. The halo effect is also a tool you can use ethically: presentation genuinely shifts how content lands, so it's worth polishing the surface, just don't mistake the polish for the substance, in others or yourself.

headline: Wittgenstein: many philosophical problems are knots in language
body: Wittgenstein came to believe that a huge share of philosophical puzzles aren't deep truths waiting to be uncovered but confusions produced by language idling, by words used outside the contexts that give them meaning. 'Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language.'
more:
His example: 'What is time?' feels like a profound mystery, but we use 'time' competently all day. The mystery appears only when we yank the word out of its ordinary use and demand a single hidden essence behind it. Look instead at how the word actually works in the 'language games' where it lives, and the fog often clears.

The practical version: when an argument feels stuck and profound, check whether everyone's using a key word the same way. 'Are video games art?' 'Is a hot dog a sandwich?' 'Is this AI conscious?' Many such debates dissolve once you notice the word is being asked to do a job it was never built for, or that the parties have quietly defined it differently. Not every problem is verbal, but spotting the ones that are saves enormous wasted effort.

headline: The Allegory of the Cave is about the pain of updating
body: Plato imagined prisoners chained facing a wall, seeing only shadows cast by objects behind them, mistaking the shadows for reality. One escapes, sees the real world and the sun, and returns to free the others. They don't thank him. Disoriented and threatened, they'd rather kill him than leave the wall.
more:
The usual reading is about enlightenment. The underrated part is the homecoming. The freed prisoner returns blinking and clumsy, worse at the shadow-game than those who never left, and the others take his confusion as proof that going up the cave ruins you. Truth doesn't arrive as triumphant clarity; it arrives as a period of looking foolish and being disbelieved.

This is the realistic shape of changing your mind, or trying to change someone else's. People who've genuinely updated often perform worse socially at first and meet hostility, not gratitude. And the prisoners aren't stupid; from inside the cave, the shadows really are all the evidence they have. The allegory is a warning to the would-be liberator as much as a promise of the light: expect resistance, and don't mistake it for proof you're wrong.

headline: Hanlon's Razor and its limits
body: 'Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity, or more charitably, by incompetence, haste, or simple constraints.' Most of the slights you take personally were never aimed at you. The late reply, the curt message, the overlooked invite, usually it's a busy distracted human, not a plot.
more:
The razor is a debiasing tool against our oversensitive threat-detection. We're wired to read agency and intent into events, so a neutral mishap feels like a deliberate strike. Defaulting to the boring explanation, overload, oversight, bad systems, saves enormous emotional energy and usually happens to be true.

But sharp tools cut their user. Hanlon's Razor fails when there's a pattern, when the 'mistakes' all conveniently benefit the same person, or when power makes 'incompetence' a free pass for the powerful. Used naively it can launder real malice as 'oh they just forgot.' The mature version: assume incompetence first, but track the pattern. One missed email is noise. The same person 'forgetting' only the inconvenient agreements is signal.

headline: Buridan's Ass: why a perfectly rational agent could starve
body: Imagine a donkey placed exactly between two identical bales of hay, equally hungry for each. With no reason to prefer one, a purely rational chooser has no basis to move, and starves. The paradox skewers the idea that every action must be backed by a decisive reason.
more:
The resolution is that good agents include a tiebreaker: when reasons are balanced, just pick. Randomize, flip a coin, go with a gut nudge. Insisting on a 'best' reason for trivially-tied choices is itself irrational, because the cost of deliberating exceeds the difference between options.

This is wildly practical. Analysis paralysis is Buridan's Ass in real life: agonizing over choices that are genuinely close, where the deliberation costs more than the wrong pick ever could. The fix is a meta-rule: for low-stakes or closely-tied decisions, optimize for deciding fast, not for deciding perfectly. Reserve heavy deliberation for choices that are both high-stakes and where the options genuinely differ. Most aren't.

headline: The Paradox of Tolerance: unlimited tolerance destroys itself
body: Karl Popper argued that a society tolerant without limit will eventually be seized by the intolerant. If you extend tolerance even to movements bent on destroying tolerance, you hand them the tools to win, and tolerance dies. So, paradoxically, a tolerant society may have to be intolerant of intolerance.
more:
Popper's version is more careful than the slogan it became. He did not say suppress every illiberal view. He argued we should counter intolerant philosophies by rational argument and keep them in check by public opinion as long as they're willing to engage at that level. Suppression is the last resort, justified only when a movement rejects argument entirely and answers reason with fists.

The distinction matters because the paradox is often misused to justify silencing mere disagreement. The real claim is narrow: tolerance is a reciprocal bargain, and you owe nothing to those who openly refuse the bargain and aim to end it by force. Where to draw that line, who counts as beyond argument, is exactly the hard and contested part the slogan skips.

headline: Sartre: you are condemned to be free
body: For Sartre, there's no fixed human essence handed to you in advance; you exist first and define yourself through your choices. That sounds liberating until you feel its weight: you can't outsource the responsibility. Even refusing to choose is a choice. Even 'I had no choice' is usually a choice you're disowning.
more:
Sartre called dodging this 'bad faith': pretending you're not free, that your role, your circumstances, or your nature decided for you. The waiter who plays at being nothing but a waiter, the person who says 'that's just how I am,' are hiding from the vertigo of authorship.

The useful, non-melodramatic takeaway: most 'I have to' statements are really 'I'm choosing this because the alternative costs more than I'll admit.' You don't have to go to that job; you're choosing it over the consequences of quitting. Naming a constraint as a choice restores agency, sometimes you'll still choose the same thing, but now you own it, and ownership is where change becomes possible. Sartre's freedom is heavy precisely because it leaves you no one else to blame.

headline: Nietzsche's eternal recurrence is a values test, not a cosmology
body: Nietzsche posed a demon's question: what if you had to live this exact life again and again, eternally, every pain and joy and boredom repeated forever in the same order? Would you curse the demon, or call it divine? He didn't claim time literally loops. He used the thought as a scale to weigh your life.
more:
The recurrence is a stress test for whether you can affirm your existence. If the thought of reliving your life fills you with dread, that's diagnostic: something is off, and you're living in a way you can't endorse. If you could embrace it, you've achieved what he called amor fati, love of fate, willing not just to accept your life but to want it exactly as it was.

Used practically, it's a clarifying question for decisions: would I want to be the kind of person who makes this choice, over and over, forever? It cuts through the temptation to live for some deferred payoff or to grit through a life you secretly reject. Nietzsche's bar is brutally high, but the question is portable and sharp: not 'is this tolerable once?' but 'would I sign up for this on infinite repeat?'

headline: Occam's Razor, done right
body: Occam's Razor is usually mangled as 'the simplest explanation is true.' It actually says: among hypotheses that explain the evidence equally well, prefer the one with the fewest assumptions. It's a tiebreaker, not a truth detector, and only fires when the candidates are otherwise equally good.
more:
The naive version causes real damage. Reality is often complicated, and the genuinely simplest story ('it was a coincidence,' 'one cause did it all') is frequently wrong. The razor doesn't say pick the simplest explanation full stop; it says don't multiply entities beyond necessity. If a complex explanation fits the evidence and the simple one doesn't, the complex one wins. Simplicity only breaks ties.

A concrete modern case: a website goes down. 'The CDN, the database, and a deploy all failed at once' versus 'a single bad deploy caused all three symptoms.' If both fit the logs equally, the single-cause story is the better bet, fewer independent coincidences. But if the logs show the database was already failing before the deploy, you don't get to wave that away for being 'simpler.' The razor is about assumptions, not about which story is shorter or more comfortable.

headline: The is-ought gap: why data never settles a values fight
body: You can establish every fact about a situation and still not have proven what anyone should do. Facts describe what is; conclusions about what we ought to do require at least one value premise. No amount of measurement bridges that gap on its own.
more:
This is the single most useful thing to know when watching arguments go in circles. Two people can fully agree on the data and still disagree on the policy, because they weight different values, liberty versus safety, present versus future, the individual versus the group. Piling on more evidence doesn't help, because the evidence was never the sticking point.

Concrete example: 'Remote work reduces commute emissions by 30%' is a fact. 'Therefore we should be remote-first' is a conclusion that secretly assumes you value emissions reduction over, say, in-person collaboration or junior-employee mentorship. The skill is to surface the hidden 'ought': when someone reasons from a study straight to a should, ask which value is doing the lifting. That's where the honest debate actually is, and it's usually one nobody has stated out loud.

headline: Falsifiability: what separates science from astrology
body: Karl Popper's criterion: a claim is scientific only if it could in principle be proven wrong. 'All swans are white' is scientific, one black swan kills it. 'Everything happens for a reason' is not, because no observation could ever count against it. A theory that explains every possible outcome explains nothing.
more:
The trap is theories that look powerful precisely because they can absorb any result. Astrology, certain conspiracy theories, and some psychological frameworks are unfalsifiable: whatever happens, the theory claims a win. 'The prediction failed because Mercury's influence was weak that week.' If nothing could ever disconfirm it, it makes no real bet about the world.

Modern test: when someone makes a confident claim, ask 'what would we expect to see if you were wrong, and have we checked?' A good forecaster, scientist, or analyst can answer crisply. A pseudo-expert can't, because their claim was built to be unsinkable. Note the nuance Popper's critics added: real science doesn't drop a theory at the first anomaly either; falsifiability is a spectrum and an ideal, not a guillotine. But 'could this ever be wrong, and how would we know?' remains one of the most clarifying questions you can ask.

headline: The map is not the territory
body: Alfred Korzybski's line: a map is a useful simplification of terrain, but it is not the terrain, and confusing the two is a category error. Every model, metric, label, and word is a map. They're indispensable, and they always leave things out, including, sometimes, the thing that matters most.
more:
The failure mode is optimizing the map until it stops matching the territory. This is Goodhart's Law in action: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Teach to the test and test scores rise while learning doesn't. Reward lines of code and you get bloated code. Track 'tickets closed' and you get tickets closed, not problems solved. The metric was a map of value; people optimized the map and abandoned the territory.

The practical discipline: never fully trust a number you can't trace back to the real thing it stands for, and periodically go look at the territory directly, talk to the actual customer, read the actual code, watch the actual user. Diagnoses, job titles, org charts, and dashboards are all maps. They're powerful precisely because they simplify, and dangerous for the exact same reason. Keep one eye on whether the map still describes the ground.

headline: Dunning-Kruger, carefully (it's not what you think)
body: The popular version, 'stupid people think they're geniuses,' is a misstatement. The actual finding is subtler: across many skills, low performers overestimate their ability and high performers slightly underestimate theirs, and almost everyone rates themselves as roughly above average. The core insight is about self-assessment, not about idiots.
more:
The real mechanism is 'dual burden': the same knowledge you'd need to be good at something is the knowledge you'd need to recognize you're bad at it. If you don't know the rules of grammar, you also can't see your own grammar errors. Incompetence is partly invisible from the inside. Crucially, the effect is modest, debated, and partly a statistical artifact, some of the pattern would appear even with random noise (regression to the mean). It is NOT a license to dismiss confident people as dumb.

The honest takeaway flips the usual smug reading. The lesson isn't 'look how clueless those overconfident people are', it's 'I am probably one of them in the domains I know least.' Your blind spots are, by definition, the places you can't see you're weak. The practical move: in any new field, assume your confidence is poorly calibrated, seek external feedback, and treat the feeling of 'this seems easy' as a possible warning sign rather than proof of talent.

headline: The Streetlight Effect: searching where the light is
body: A drunk man searches for his keys under a streetlight. A passerby helps, then asks if he's sure he dropped them here. 'No, I dropped them in the park, but the light's better here.' We systematically look for answers where they're easy to look, not where they're likely to be found.
more:
It's everywhere data is available but the truth isn't. We measure what's easy to measure and then quietly redefine the problem to match. Companies optimize click-through rates because they're trackable, even when the real goal, customer satisfaction or long-term trust, is harder to see. Medicine long studied whichever diseases had easy markers. Researchers chase questions with available datasets rather than important ones.

The practical defense: separate 'what's important' from 'what's measurable' and notice when they've drifted apart. Before trusting an analysis, ask: is this addressing the real question, or just the part that happened to have good lighting? Sometimes the honest answer is 'the key data doesn't exist,' and acknowledging that beats a confident answer built entirely from the convenient subset. The streetlight isn't useless, the keys might be there. But systematically only searching the lit area guarantees you miss everything in the dark.

headline: The genetic fallacy: where an idea came from doesn't decide if it's true
body: The genetic fallacy is judging a claim by its origin rather than its content. 'That idea came from a company trying to sell something, so it's false.' 'He's biased, so he's wrong.' The source may be a reason for suspicion, but it's not, by itself, a refutation. Bad people can state true things; good people can be wrong.
more:
It cuts both ways, including the flattering direction: 'this comes from a famous scientist, so it's true' is the same fallacy in reverse. The origin of a claim is evidence about how carefully to check it, not a substitute for checking it. A self-interested source warrants scrutiny; it doesn't settle the question.

Concrete modern version: 'this health advice comes from a supplement company, ignore it.' The financial interest is a real red flag and a reason to verify independently, but the advice itself is either supported by evidence or not, and that's what determines the truth. The discipline is to use the source to set your level of scrutiny, then actually evaluate the content. Dismissing ideas purely by tribe, funding, or messenger feels like critical thinking but is often just a way to avoid engaging with an inconvenient argument.

headline: Survivorship bias: the data that didn't make it back
body: In WWII, analysts examined returning bombers to decide where to add armor, marking the planes' bullet holes, concentrated on wings and tail. The instinct was to reinforce those spots. Statistician Abraham Wald saw the opposite: armor the UNHIT areas, the engines and cockpit. Planes hit there never came back to be studied.
more:
The returning planes were a biased sample, the survivors. The absence of damage in a spot didn't mean it was safe; it meant hits there were fatal. We constantly reason from survivors and forget the silent population that didn't make it into our dataset.

This is the hidden flaw in most success advice. 'Successful founders dropped out of college, so dropping out works' ignores the vastly larger group who dropped out and failed, who don't write books. 'These habits made me rich' studies only the rich. Old buildings seem better built, but we only see the ones that lasted. The practical reflex: whenever you're learning from a set of successes, ask 'where are the failures, and would I even be able to see them?' The most important data is often the data that, by its nature, never shows up.

headline: Steelmanning: argue against the best version, not the worst
body: A straw man is a weak caricature of your opponent's view that's easy to knock down. Steelmanning is the opposite: before you disagree, reconstruct their argument in its strongest, most charitable form, sometimes stronger than they stated it, and then engage with that. You attack the steel, not the straw.
more:
It's not just politeness; it's epistemic self-interest. If you can only beat a weak version of the opposing view, you've learned nothing and proven nothing. If you can defeat the strongest version, your own position is genuinely robust, and if you can't, you've discovered you might be wrong, which is the whole point of thinking.

Practically, steelmanning is a forcing function against the comfortable feeling of being obviously right. Before dismissing a coworker's proposal, a policy, or a rival approach, try to state the case for it so well that its advocates would say 'yes, exactly.' Often you'll find a real consideration you'd been ignoring. The bonus: people are far more willing to update when they feel understood first, so steelmanning is also the most persuasive way to disagree. The version of an argument worth defeating is the one a smart, honest person would actually make.

headline: Epistemic humility: calibrating confidence to evidence
body: Epistemic humility isn't wishy-washy 'nobody can really know anything.' It's the discipline of matching your confidence to your actual evidence, being very sure where the evidence is strong, genuinely uncertain where it's thin, and able to say 'I don't know' without it feeling like defeat.
more:
The opposite is not confidence; it's miscalibration, being equally certain about things you've studied for years and things you skimmed once. Good thinkers hold beliefs with a 'confidence dial,' and they can tell you roughly how sure they are and what would change their mind. The phrase 'I might be wrong, and here's what would convince me' is a mark of strength, not weakness.

Concrete practice: attach probabilities, even rough ones, to your predictions, and check them later. People who do this discover they're systematically overconfident, and improve. In a meeting, distinguish 'I'm 95% sure' from 'I'd guess, maybe 60%', it changes how others should weight you and how hard you should push. Real expertise often shows up as more hedging, not less, because experts can see the edges of what they know. Loud certainty is frequently a sign of not knowing where those edges are.

headline: The Sunk Cost Fallacy: the past is not a reason
body: We keep pouring resources into failing endeavors because of what we've already spent, the half-finished project, the years in the wrong career, the movie we're not enjoying but already paid for. But spent resources are gone whatever you do next. Only future costs and benefits should drive the decision.
more:
The rational rule is brutally simple: ignore what's already invested; ask only 'from here forward, is continuing the best use of my remaining time and money?' What you've sunk is irrelevant to that question, because you can't get it back by either choice. Yet we feel that quitting would 'waste' the investment, when in fact continuing wastes even more.

The trap is wired deep, we hate admitting a loss, and stopping feels like confirming we were wrong. Governments do it with doomed mega-projects ('we've spent too much to stop now', which is exactly backwards). The practical antidote: imagine you were just handed the current situation fresh, with no history. Would you start this project today? If not, the only thing keeping you in is the sunk cost, and that's not a reason, it's a feeling wearing a reason's clothes. Note the honest caveat: reputation and commitment can be real future costs, those count. The fallacy is counting the past itself.

headline: Quiz: What does Chesterton's Fence actually advise?
body: You inherit a system with a confusing rule that seems pointless. According to Chesterton's Fence, what should you do?
options: Remove it immediately, since anything without obvious purpose is waste
Keep it forever, because old rules are wiser than new ones
Understand why it was put there before deciding whether to remove it
Ask a vote of the majority and follow whatever they prefer
explanation: Chesterton's Fence is a sequencing rule, not a conservative one. It says: figure out why the fence exists before tearing it down. Once you genuinely understand the reason, you may well remove it, the principle isn't 'never change things,' it's 'don't remove what you don't yet understand.'

headline: Quiz: The is-ought gap implies which of these?
body: Two analysts agree completely on all the data about a policy but still disagree on whether to adopt it. The is-ought gap suggests the most likely explanation is:
options: One of them is misreading the data and needs to recheck the numbers
They weight different underlying values, which no amount of data resolves
Values don't exist, so the disagreement is meaningless
More data will eventually force them to agree
explanation: Hume's point is that facts alone never entail an 'ought.' If two people share all the facts and still disagree on what to do, the disagreement lives in their values, not the data, which is exactly why throwing more evidence at a values dispute rarely settles it.

headline: Quiz: Which claim is unfalsifiable?
body: By Popper's criterion, which of these statements is NOT scientific because nothing could ever count against it?
options: Objects fall toward Earth at about 9.8 meters per second squared
This drug lowers blood pressure more than a placebo
Everything that happens was meant to happen, for reasons we may not see
The universe is expanding and galaxies are moving apart
explanation: 'Everything was meant to happen' is compatible with literally any observation, no event could ever disconfirm it, so it makes no real prediction. The other three each specify what we'd expect to see and could be proven wrong by contrary measurements. Falsifiability is what gives a claim empirical teeth.

headline: Quiz: What does the Dunning-Kruger effect actually claim?
body: Which statement most accurately describes the Dunning-Kruger effect as the research actually found it?
options: Stupid people believe they are geniuses, while smart people know they're smart
Low performers tend to overestimate their ability because they lack the knowledge to see their own gaps
Confidence and competence are perfectly inversely related
Experts are always less confident than beginners in every field
explanation: The real finding is about self-assessment: the same knowledge needed to perform well is needed to judge your own performance, so low performers can't see their own gaps. It's modest, debated, and partly a statistical artifact, and it implies YOU are likely miscalibrated in your weakest domains, not that 'other people are idiots.'

headline: Quiz: Spot the survivorship bias
body: Which conclusion is most distorted by survivorship bias?
options: A controlled trial randomly assigns patients and tracks every one of them
'Most billionaires wake at 5am, so waking at 5am helps you get rich'
A census attempts to count every household in a country
An engineer tests components to failure and records all results
explanation: Studying only billionaires ignores the enormous number of early risers who never got rich, the failures don't make the sample. Without the people who did the same thing and failed, you can't tell if the habit caused success or is just noise. The other options deliberately include the full population, success and failure alike.

headline: Quiz: The Experience Machine is an argument against what?
body: Nozick's Experience Machine, the device that gives you perfect pleasurable experiences while you float in a tank, is primarily an argument against which view?
options: Determinism, the idea that all events are caused
Hedonism, the idea that pleasure is the only thing that matters
Dualism, the idea that mind and body are separate
Relativism, the idea that truth is relative
explanation: If pleasurable experience were all we valued, plugging in would be obvious. Most people refuse, which suggests we value actually doing things and actually connecting with reality, not just the feeling of it. That's a direct strike against hedonism's claim that pleasure is the sole good.

headline: Quiz: The map is not the territory, applied
body: A school ties teacher bonuses to standardized test scores. Scores rise sharply, but independent assessments show students aren't actually learning more. Which principle best explains this?
options: Occam's Razor, the simplest explanation is correct
The genetic fallacy, judging a claim by its source
Goodhart's Law, when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure
The halo effect, one good trait colors all judgments
explanation: The test score was a map of learning. Once it became the target, people optimized the map, teaching to the test, and abandoned the territory, actual learning. This is Goodhart's Law, the practical edge of 'the map is not the territory.' Good metrics decay the moment they become the thing you're rewarded for hitting.

headline: Quiz: Which is the sunk cost fallacy?
body: Which reasoning is an example of the sunk cost fallacy?
options: 'This project will cost more to finish than it will ever return, so let's stop'
'We've already spent two years on this, so we have to see it through even though it's clearly failing'
'Quitting now would damage relationships we'll need later, and that future cost is large'
'Starting fresh, would we choose this path today? No, so let's change course'
explanation: Only option 2 treats already-spent resources as a reason to continue, which is the fallacy, that money and time are gone either way. Option 3 isn't the fallacy because reputation is a real FUTURE cost. Options 1 and 4 are exactly the correct, forward-looking way to decide.

headline: Quiz: What is steelmanning?
body: Before disagreeing with a colleague, you restate their proposal in its strongest possible form, even adding a point they missed, then respond to that. What are you doing, and why is it smart?
options: Straw-manning, because exaggerating their view makes it easier to dismiss
Steelmanning, because defeating the strongest version is the only result worth anything
The genetic fallacy, because you're focusing on who said it
Begging the question, because you assume your conclusion
explanation: Steelmanning means engaging the strongest version of an opposing view. It's epistemic self-interest: if you can only beat a weak caricature you've proven nothing, and if you can't beat the strong version, you've usefully learned you might be wrong. As a bonus, people update more readily when they feel understood first.

headline: Puzzle: The Sorites Paradox (the heap)
body: A heap of sand has, say, a million grains. Remove one grain, it's still a heap. Removing a single grain never turns a heap into a non-heap. But repeat the step enough times and you reach one grain, or zero, clearly not a heap. Each step seems valid, yet the conclusion is absurd. Where does the reasoning break?
answer: The paradox exposes that 'heap' is a vague predicate with no sharp boundary, and our logic quietly assumes every term has crisp edges. The flawed premise is 'removing one grain never changes a heap to a non-heap': stated as an absolute rule it's false, even if no single removal is the obvious culprit. There is no precise grain count where heap-ness switches off, because 'heap' was never defined that finely; it has a fuzzy borderline zone where 'heap' and 'not a heap' both half-apply. Several formal fixes exist, fuzzy logic assigns degrees of truth (a 30-grain pile is 'sort of' a heap); supervaluationism says it's indeterminate in the gray zone; the epistemic view holds there IS a sharp line but it's unknowable to us. The practical lesson is bigger than sand: most useful words, bald, tall, rich, addicted, fair, are sorites-vague, and demanding a precise cutoff ('exactly how many hairs make someone not bald?') is a confusion, not a deep question. Vagueness is a feature of language, not a flaw to be argued away.

headline: Puzzle: The Unexpected Hanging
body: A judge tells a prisoner: 'You'll be hanged at noon on one weekday next week, but the day will be a surprise, you won't know which morning until the executioner comes.' The prisoner reasons: it can't be Friday, since by Thursday night I'd know. So not Thursday either, by the same logic. He eliminates every day, concludes he can't be hanged at all, and relaxes. Then on Wednesday they hang him, completely surprised. Where did his airtight logic go wrong?
answer: This is one of philosophy's genuinely unresolved puzzles, no consensus fix exists, but the most compelling diagnosis is self-reference. The prisoner's elimination argument uses the assumption 'the sentence will be carried out' to prove the sentence can't be carried out, which is incoherent: if his reasoning were sound, it would refute its own premise, and then the premise it relied on collapses. Many logicians argue the judge's statement is subtly self-undermining, like 'this sentence is a surprise', it can't be fully known by the prisoner without becoming false, yet remains true from the judge's side. The cleanest practical reading: 'surprise' means the prisoner can't deduce the day with certainty in advance. The backward-induction argument feels like a proof but secretly requires the prisoner to already be certain of things he can't actually be certain of. Once he's 'proven' he's safe, that very confidence makes ANY day a surprise again, including the ones he ruled out. His error was trusting a chain of reasoning whose conclusion destroyed its own foundation. The deeper lesson: arguments that loop back to undermine their own premises can look valid step-by-step while being globally broken.

headline: Puzzle: The Liar Paradox
body: Consider the sentence: 'This sentence is false.' If it's true, then what it says holds, so it's false. But if it's false, then it's not the case that it's false, so it's true. It flips endlessly, true implies false implies true. A single innocent sentence breaks the basic rule that every statement is either true or false. What's going on?
answer: The liar shows that natural language lets you build sentences that talk about their own truth, and self-reference plus negation can produce a value that's neither stably true nor stably false. The standard modern responses don't 'solve' it so much as fence it off. Tarski argued that no consistent language can contain its own complete truth predicate; you need a hierarchy, statements at one level can only be called true or false from a higher level, which forbids the liar's self-application. Others reject bivalence (the assumption that every sentence must be exactly true OR false): the liar is simply neither, a truth-value 'gap,' or in dialetheist views, a rare sentence that's both at once. Kripke's influential approach treats such sentences as 'ungrounded', they never get a truth value because there's nothing to anchor them to. The shared insight: the paradox isn't a flaw in reality but a sign that 'true' and 'false' have limits, and a language flexible enough to discuss its own truth will inevitably contain sentences it cannot consistently evaluate. The practical echo shows up in computing as undecidability and the halting problem, the same self-reference trap, formalized.

headline: Marcus Aurelius ran an empire and journaled to stay sane. His tools still work →
body: The most powerful man in the Roman world wrote a private notebook he never meant anyone to read, reminders to himself on how to not be ruined by power, fear, anger, and other people. We call it the Meditations. It's less a treatise than a self-help log from someone with every excuse to become a monster who was trying hard not to. Four of his practical mental tools, ahead.

headline: Tool 1: The view from above
body: When overwhelmed, Marcus would zoom out, mentally rising until cities looked like anthills, his lifespan a blink against geological time, his crisis one of countless that humans have weathered and forgotten. Not to feel small in despair, but to right-size a panic that had inflated to fill his whole sky.
more: The technique works because anxiety collapses your perspective onto a single threat until it feels infinite. Deliberately widening the frame, this will matter little in a year, billions have faced worse, the sun will rise regardless, doesn't deny the problem; it restores proportion. A modern version: when a work crisis has your stomach in knots, ask where it ranks against the actual scale of your life and the world. Usually it shrinks to manageable. Marcus used cosmic scale to keep imperial-sized problems from feeling like the end of everything.

headline: Tool 2: Other people's faults are not your character
body: Marcus's recurring morning rehearsal: 'Today I'll meet people who are ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous.' He prepared for the worst not to become cynical, but so that bad behavior couldn't ambush him, and so he could remember that another person's vice harms his own character only if he lets it provoke him into matching it.
more: The insight is that you can't control who you'll deal with, but you control whether their behavior pulls you down to it. An idiot cutting you off in traffic only ruins your day if you hand them that power. Marcus kept returning to the idea that the best revenge, and the best self-protection, is to not be like the person who wronged you. He also pushed himself to consider that the offender often acts from ignorance, not malice, and genuinely believes they're in the right, which makes anger at them as misplaced as anger at someone who's simply mistaken.

headline: Tool 3: Objective description strips the drama
body: Marcus practiced describing things in plain, deflated terms to see them without the story we layer on. Fine wine is 'fermented grape juice.' A luxurious feast is 'dead animals and plants.' Sex is 'friction and a spasm.' The point wasn't to ruin pleasure but to see how much of an object's grip on us comes from the narrative around it, not the thing itself.
more: By stripping the marketing, the status, the hype, the manufactured longing, from a thing, you can judge whether you actually want it or just want what you've been told it means. It's a direct antidote to consumer craving and status anxiety: that watch is metal and gears; that promotion is a different label and a different set of headaches. Used in reverse, the same trick can de-escalate dread, the terrifying confrontation is 'two people exchanging sounds in a room.' Seeing things stripped of their inflated story gives you back the choice of how much they should move you.

headline: Tool 4: You only ever have the present
body: Marcus kept reminding himself that no one loses the past or the future, since you can't lose what you don't have; you only ever possess this present moment. Even a person who lives a hundred years and one who dies young lose exactly the same thing when they die, the present, because that's all anyone ever has to lose.
more: The practical force is twofold. First, almost all suffering is time-travel, dread of a future that hasn't come or regret over a past you can't touch. Returning attention to the only moment you can actually act in is where Stoicism and modern mindfulness shake hands. Second, it reframes mortality: if all you ever hold is the present, then a long life doesn't grant you 'more' of life to lose, only more present moments lived. It's a strangely steadying thought from a man who knew he could die of plague or assassination any day, and chose to spend his actual moments doing his duty rather than fearing their end.

headline: Your memory is a rewrite, not a replay
body: Every time you recall an event, you partially reconstruct it from fragments and beliefs about how things 'must have' gone. Then you re-store that slightly edited version. Memory is less like opening a saved file and more like retelling a story you can't help embellishing.
more:
Elizabeth Loftus showed how easily this goes wrong. In her studies, simply asking witnesses how fast cars were going when they 'smashed' versus 'hit' each other changed their speed estimates and even made some 'remember' broken glass that was never there.

This is why confident eyewitness testimony has sent innocent people to prison. The Innocence Project found that mistaken identification was a factor in a large majority of DNA exonerations. Confidence and accuracy are only loosely related once a memory has been disturbed.

headline: Consistency bias: editing your past self to match today
